entry: Irish playwright, critic, polemicist, and political activist. Born in Dublin, Shaw moved to London in 1876 and became a respected theatre and music critic by the mid-1880s. Influenced by [[Henrik Ibsen|Ibsen]], he used his plays to promote his political, social, and religious ideas. His successes included *Major Barbara*, *Pygmalion* (1913), and *Saint Joan* (1923), and he wrote more than 60 plays. He won the 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature and an Academy Award for the 1938 film version of *Pygmalion*. Shaw promoted [[Eugenics|eugenics]] and alphabet reform, opposed vaccination, and in later years expressed admiration for both [[Benito Mussolini|Mussolini]] and [[Joseph Stalin|Stalin]]. He courted unpopularity by denouncing both sides in the First World War as equally culpable.

Northern Irish footballer, a right winger who spent most of his club career at Manchester United. Born in [[Belfast]], he scored 179 goals in 470 appearances for the club and won two League titles and the European Cup. Named European Footballer of the Year in 1968, he became one of the first media [[Celebrity|celebrity]] footballers. He was capped 37 times for Northern Ireland but never played in the finals of a major tournament. [[Alcoholism]] affected him on and off the field for the rest of his life, and he died of complications from immunosuppressive drugs taken after a 2002 liver transplant.

English mathematician and philosopher. Largely self-taught in mathematics after becoming the family breadwinner at 16, Boole transformed [[Logic|logic]] from a philosophical study of language into a mathematical system of algebraic equations using binary values and logical operators. In 1847 he developed [[Boolean algebra]], which is contained in *The Laws of Thought* (1854). In 1849 he became the first professor of mathematics at Queen's College, [[Cork (city)|Cork]], in Ireland. [[Claude Shannon]] and Victor Shestakov later used Boolean algebra to optimize electromechanical relay systems, a step that led to modern electronic digital computers. Boolean logic is credited with helping to lay the foundations of the [[Information Age]]. He received the Royal Society's first gold prize for mathematics and the Keith Medal.

American comedian, actor, writer, and singer, born Nathan Birnbaum in [[New York City]]. His career spanned [[Vaudeville|vaudeville]], radio, film, and television, and with his wife, Gracie Allen, he formed the comedy duo Burns and Allen. His arched eyebrow and cigar smoke became trademarks. At age 79 he revived his career in *The Sunshine Boys* (1975), winning the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor. He later played [[God]] in the *Oh, God!* films.

American military officer and diplomat. As Chief of Staff of the U.S. Army during [[World War II]], he coordinated Allied operations and was promoted to five-star rank as General of the Army. [[Winston Churchill]] praised him as the "organizer of victory." As Secretary of State from 1947 to 1949, he advocated European recovery, and the Marshall Plan bears his name. It earned him the 1953 Nobel Peace Prize, the only Army general to receive it. In 1945–1947 he was a special envoy to China, seeking unsuccessfully to form a coalition between the Nationalists of [[Chiang Kai-shek]] and the Communists of [[Mao Zedong]]. As Secretary of Defense after the [[Korean War]] began, he worked to restore the military's confidence and morale.

American stage and screen actor. Known for stern but complex authority figures, Scott won the Academy Award for Best Actor for playing General George S. Patton in *Patton* (1970) but became the first actor to decline the award, arguing that performances cannot be compared. His other Oscar-nominated films include *Anatomy of a Murder* (1959) and *The Hustler* (1961), and his notable films also include *Dr. Strangelove* (1964). He won two Primetime Emmy Awards, for his performances in *Hallmark Hall of Fame* (1971) and *12 Angry Men* (1997).

American stand-up comedian, satirist, social critic, actor, and author. His routines combined dark comedy with commentary on politics, language, psychology, and religion, and from the late 1980s focused on criticism of American society. His "seven dirty words" routine was central to the 1978 Supreme Court case FCC v. Pacifica Foundation, in which a 5–4 decision affirmed the government's power to censor indecent material on public airwaves. He hosted the first episode of [[Saturday Night Live]] in 1975 and was a frequent performer on *The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson*. He made 14 stand-up specials for [[HBO]] and won five [[Grammy Awards]] for Best Comedy Album.

American actor and filmmaker. He broke through as Dr. Doug Ross in the NBC medical drama [[ER (TV series)|ER]] (1994–1999) and won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for *Syriana* (2005). He received the Academy Award for Best Picture as a producer of *Argo* (2012). He has directed nine feature films, including *Good Night, and Good Luck* (2005). He has been a United Nations Messenger of Peace since 2008 and is noted for political and economic [[Activism|activism]].

British statesman, Conservative politician, explorer, and writer. [[India|Viceroy of India]] from 1899 to 1905, he pursued administrative reforms and undertook the restoration of the [[Taj Mahal]]. In 1905 he presided over the partition of Bengal and resigned that year after a clash with Lord Kitchener over military organization. As Foreign Secretary from 1919 to 1924, he was chief Allied negotiator of the 1922 Treaty of Lausanne, which defined the borders of modern [[Turkey]]. His name was given to the Curzon Line, Britain's proposed Soviet-Polish boundary. Earlier he traveled widely in [[Russia]], Central Asia, and the Far East, and wrote about the perceived Russian threat to British control of India.

American innovator and entrepreneur, founder of the Eastman Kodak Company. He helped bring roll film into the mainstream. After a decade of experiments he patented and sold a roll-film camera, making amateur photography accessible to the general public. The 1888 Kodak camera was sold loaded with enough film for 100 exposures; the photographer mailed it back to the company, which processed the film and returned the camera with prints. As treasurer and later president of Kodak, he oversaw the company's expansion. He endowed the Eastman School of Music, the [[Rochester, New York|Rochester]] Philharmonic Orchestra, and dental and medical schools at the University of Rochester, and he made large gifts to the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], Tuskegee University, and Hampton University.

English novelist, poet, journalist, and translator, born Mary Ann Evans. One of the leading writers of the [[Victorian era|Victorian era]], she wrote seven novels, including *Adam Bede* (1859), *The Mill on the Floss* (1860), and *Silas Marner* (1861). Her novels are known for their realism, psychological insight, and detailed depiction of the countryside. *Middlemarch* (1871–1872) was called by [[Virginia Woolf]] "one of the few English novels written for grown-up people." From 1854 to 1878 she lived with the married critic George Henry Lewes, an unconventional arrangement for the era. In 1880, 18 months after Lewes's death, she married her longtime friend John Cross.

American boxer, minister, businessman, and author. Olympic heavyweight gold medalist in 1968, he won the undisputed world heavyweight title in 1973 by knocking out [[Joe Frazier]] in the second round. He lost the title to [[Muhammad Ali]] in 1974 and retired after losing to Jimmy Young in 1977. Ordained as a Christian minister, he returned to boxing and at age 45 regained the unified WBA, IBF, and lineal heavyweight titles in 1994. The George Foreman Grill, which bears his name, sold more than 100 million units worldwide by 2011.

German-British Baroque composer. Known for [[Opera|operas]], oratorios, anthems, concerti grossi, and organ concerti, he brought Italian opera to its highest development and created the English oratorio and organ concerto. Born in Halle, he spent time in Hamburg and Italy before settling in London in 1712, becoming a naturalized British subject in 1727. After the success of *Messiah* (1742), he never composed another Italian opera. His music was admired by Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven. His *Water Music* and *Music for the Royal Fireworks* remain popular, and his anthem *Zadok the Priest* has been performed at every British coronation since 1727. He was given a state funeral at [[Westminster Abbey]].

American composer and pianist of [[Jazz|jazz]], popular, and classical music. His songs included "Swanee" (1919) and "I Got Rhythm" (1930). His orchestral works *Rhapsody in Blue* (1924) and *An American in Paris* (1928) blended jazz idioms with concert forms. He wrote the opera *Porgy and Bess* (1935), which included the hit "Summertime." Initially a commercial failure, it came to be considered one of the most important American operas of the 20th century. His *Of Thee I Sing* (1931) was the first musical to win the Pulitzer Prize for Drama. [[Nadia Boulanger]] refused to teach him, fearing that rigorous study would ruin his jazz-influenced style, and [[Maurice Ravel]] voiced similar objections. He also wrote film scores in Hollywood.

Philosopher, mystic, composer, and spiritual teacher. Born in Alexandropol in the [[Russian Empire]], he taught that people live in a hypnotic "waking sleep" and can awaken to a higher consciousness in order to "remember ourselves." His pupil P. D. Ouspensky called his teachings the "Fourth Way." Gurdjieff also composed music and taught movements, or sacred dances. After his death, the Gurdjieff Foundation in Paris was established under his pupil Jeanne de Salzmann, and groups formed in many countries.

[[President of the United States|41st president of the United States]], 1989–1993. He had served as the 43rd vice president under [[Ronald Reagan]] from 1981 to 1989, and earlier as Director of Central Intelligence and U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. Foreign policy drove his presidency: he played a key role in German reunification and in the [[Gulf War]] that ended Iraq's occupation of Kuwait. He signed the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, but raised taxes to reduce the budget deficit despite a 1988 campaign pledge. He lost the 1992 election to [[Bill Clinton]]. He was the father of [[George W. Bush]].

English musician and member of [[The Beatles]], known as the "Quiet Beatle." He played lead guitar and later bass, organ, and sitar, and wrote songs including "Something" and "Here Comes the Sun." After the band broke up, his triple album *All Things Must Pass* produced his biggest hit, "My Sweet Lord." He organized the 1971 Concert for Bangladesh with [[Ravi Shankar]], a precursor to benefit concerts such as [[Live Aid]]. In 1988 he co-founded the Traveling Wilburys with [[Roy Orbison]], [[Bob Dylan]], and [[Tom Petty]].

King of Great Britain and Ireland, 1760–1820, and duke and prince-elector of Hanover, becoming King of Hanover in 1814. He was the first Hanoverian monarch born in Britain, and English was his first language. Early in his reign Britain defeated France in the [[Seven Years' War]], but it lost 13 North American colonies in the American War of Independence. Wars against revolutionary and Napoleonic France ended with Napoleon's defeat at the [[Battle of Waterloo]] in 1815. The Acts of Union created the [[United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland]], and the [[Atlantic slave trade|transatlantic slave trade]] was banned from the British Empire in 1807. In later life he suffered recurrent, then permanent, mental illness, possibly bipolar disorder or porphyria, and his son became Prince Regent in 1811. He married Princess Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz and had 15 children with her. At his death he was the longest-lived and longest-reigning British monarch, having reigned 59 years and 96 days.

King of Great Britain and Ireland, 1727–1760, and Elector of [[Hanover]]. Born in Hanover, he was the most recent British monarch born outside Britain. Parliament largely controlled domestic policy, but later scholarship concludes that he influenced foreign policy and military appointments more than earlier historians believed. He took part in the Battle of Dettingen during the [[War of the Austrian Succession]], becoming the most recent British monarch to lead an army in battle. He was succeeded by his grandson, [[George III]].

King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, 1820–1830. He had been prince regent for his father, [[George III]], from 1811 during the king's mental illness. He commissioned John Nash to build the Royal Pavilion in [[Brighton]] and the rebuilding of [[Windsor Castle]]. His extravagance and poor relationship with his wife, Caroline of Brunswick, earned him public contempt; he excluded her from his coronation. Under Lord Liverpool's government, Britain achieved its ultimate victory over [[Napoleon]], but George was forced to accept Catholic emancipation, which he had opposed.

King of Great Britain and Ireland, 1714–1727, and Elector of [[Hanover]]. He was the first British monarch of the House of Hanover, inheriting the throne as the senior Protestant descendant of [[James VI and I]]. During his reign the powers of the monarchy diminished, and Britain moved toward cabinet government led by a prime minister. [[Robert Walpole]], now recognized as Britain's first de facto prime minister, held much of the real political power toward the end of the reign. Jacobites attempted, but failed, to depose him. He died on a journey to Hanover, where he was buried, and was succeeded by his son George II.

American filmmaker, philanthropist, and entrepreneur. He created the *Star Wars* franchise and, with [[Steven Spielberg]], the *Indiana Jones* films, and he founded Lucasfilm, Industrial Light & Magic, and THX. After co-founding American Zoetrope with [[Francis Ford Coppola]], he directed *American Graffiti* (1973), which received five Academy Award nominations. *Star Wars* (1977) became the highest-grossing film at the time and won six Academy Awards. He produced the sequels *The Empire Strikes Back* (1980) and *Return of the Jedi* (1983). He is considered one of the most significant figures of the [[New Hollywood]] movement. He sold Lucasfilm to [[The Walt Disney Company]] in 2012 and has since focused on philanthropy.

English [[Mountaineering|mountaineer]] who took part in the first three British expeditions to [[Mount Everest|Everest]] in the early 1920s. On the 1922 expedition his team set a world altitude record of 27,300 ft (8,321 m) using supplemental oxygen. On the 1924 expedition he and Andrew "Sandy" Irvine were last seen near the summit, and whether they reached it remains unknown. Mallory's body was found on the mountain in 1999, but it provided no evidence that he had reached the summit. He is remembered for his reply, "Because it's there," when asked why he wanted to climb Everest.

English singer-songwriter and record producer. He rose to fame as the lead vocalist of the pop duo Wham!, formed with Andrew Ridgeley in 1981. His solo debut, *Faith* (1987), won the [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] for Album of the Year and sold more than 25 million copies. He performed at [[Live Aid]] in 1985. He came out as gay in 1998 and was an active LGBTQ rights campaigner and [[HIV/AIDS|HIV/AIDS]] charity fundraiser. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2023. He had 13 number-one songs in the UK and 10 on the US Billboard Hot 100.

English novelist, poet, essayist, journalist, and critic, born Eric Arthur Blair. He is best known for the allegorical novella *Animal Farm* (1945) and the dystopian novel *Nineteen Eighty-Four* (1949). His writing opposed all [[Totalitarianism|totalitarianism]], both authoritarian communism and [[Fascism|fascism]], and supported [[Democratic socialism|democratic socialism]]. *Homage to Catalonia* (1938), about his service for the Republican side in the [[Spanish Civil War]], and *The Road to Wigan Pier* (1937) combined reportage with social criticism. Terms from his novels, including "Big Brother," "Newspeak," and "doublethink," entered the English language. His essays on politics, literature, and language are as critically respected as his fiction. In 2008, *The Times* named him the second-greatest British writer since 1945.
